item.title: Three Villages in a Trenchcoat, Post I
item.description:
Epistemic Status: 15 years working as a therapist, 6+ of them with rationalist and EA clients. 7 years teaching and directing at rationality camps and workshops, and many more as a member of several of this community's overlapping subcultures.

Disclaimer: I finished my first draft of this article and its two subsequent ones months ago and sent them out for feedback to various people before a bunch of stuff happened in my life that derailed me from finishing, and in the meantime, a big ol' brouhaha started around Slutcon 2 and various frictions this article was meant to highlight within the rationalist and EA community surfaced in The Discourse.

All of which is to say, this post is explicitly not about any specific incident, and deliberately avoids litigating any. It's a guide to the structural dynamics that make such situations arise; where I make claims about how things go wrong and why, I'm drawing on a mix of research, observations, and both clinical and non-clinical experiences within these communities and beyond them.

TL;DR: It's helpful to think of the rationality/EA community as a village (social scene, professional network, dating pool, housing market, all tied together by shared culture and communal events), but it's also ultimately misleading.

We have never had the stabilizing infrastructure or monoculture that helps people navigate dual roles and boundary crossings that traditionally occur in real villages, and we've grown big enough to split into subcommunities with their own social norms and expectations that cause friction at the interfaces.

Also, traditional villages kind of suck in a number of ways we don’t want to copy, but we should understand the failure modes inherent to this fairly unique confluence of circumstances to try and navigate them better.

Three Villages in a Trenchcoat

Say you’re at one of those infamous Berkeley house parties. Around the kitchen table are someone who might fund your org, a writer whose blog got you into all this, someone you dated last spring, your housemate’s ex who's now dating your coworker, and someone who’ll have a say in whether you get a room in a group house you’ve been eyeing. Most know each other, a few of them have dated each other, and at some point one might invite you to cuddle, or ask you to go for a walk, or offer you something to drink, and what that means will depend on which of several overlapping subcultures they learned their norms in.

For a lot of people in the Rationalist/Effective Altruist/Postrat/EA-adjacent/etc community (hereafter referred to as some variation of "the community" or "the village"), that’s a fairly ordinary part of the social landscape. But it's certainly not one any of us grew up learning to navigate, or even heard about, because it's something that's actually quite new and unique.

This isn't an article about Berkeley, but what happens when social scenes become sufficiently village-like. London, Boston, Berlin, EAGs, Vibecamp, and other community hubs sit at different points on the same graph.

It also isn't meant as a guide purely for newcomers; even if you've been to plenty of conferences and parties, your first time in a new part of the scene can put you in practically the same position as the newcomer, or an even worse one if you're overconfident you know the local norms.

If this first article does its job well it'll help everyone, from newcomer to veteran, have a better sense of what this big, beautiful community that's grown around us actually is and isn't, and help us navigate our differences better for all involved... though that part will mostly be covered in the later posts.

But first, why the "village" frame at all?

1) Multi-role density

Quick check: what's your "village quotient" for the community?

  • Is it where you work, or sometimes find work, or find funding for work?
  • Do you live with people who are also in it?
  • How many of your closest friends or partners are in it?
  • What portion of social events do you look forward to that are part of it?
  • How much does it contribute to your intellectual or philosophical identity or sense of life-purpose?

Modern urban life, which shapes the default culture for most Americans and Europeans, just doesn’t have protocols for a social system where employers, neighbors, friends, partners and exes, therapists/lifecoaches/priests, and so on all work and live on the same few blocks.

The standard advice to “keep your professional and personal lives separate” comes from a very modern culture that never intentionally decided to build separation into day-to-day life. Instead people just started becoming aware of many kinds of drama that can come from mixed roles and developed heuristics against them, even though the drama mostly came from other factors, and threw out whole categories of basic social interaction along the way... at least, when they could get away with it. There’s a whole area of rural-practice literature for dual-role-sensitive professions like lawyers and police and therapists because dual relationships there are unavoidable.

But real villages, and the small bands we evolved in before forming them, don't have those separation, and managed to be very functional, because role crossing is not in and of itself an actual problem; the problem is how role crossings are handled, and real villages have stabilizing infrastructure to navigate them.

Infrastructure our community largely lacks, namely:

  • One broadly shared set of norms that everyone grew up learning the rules to.
  • Elders whose judgment carried both experience and authority.
  • Gossip networks that everyone knew about and participated in.
  • Kinship stakes that made people think twice about anti-social behavior.
  • Reputational consequences that were fairly predictable.
  • Rites of passage that marked when you were expected to know your own mind and answer for your choices.

Sure, our village has some version of some of these things. We have gossip networks, but lack common knowledge and shared agreement about how they should function, which makes them hard to predict or participate in as needed.

Small towns still run on a version of that sort of intangible infrastructure, and they mostly work because there are stabilizers in rough proportion to the entanglement: shared norms, long memories, low churn.

Our young, cobbled together village never had those. Instead we have weak and perpetually contested enforcement of norms that no one ever formally agreed on, constant churn of members both by self-labeling and geography (including an annual influx of very smart young people from a variety of backgrounds and cultures), and a dating pool and job market overlap to our friendgroups that virtually none of us were raised to know how to socially navigate.

And all this might work if our shared ideology was a very conservative, tradition-oriented one. Instead we share an ideology that drives us to poke at Chesterton Fences and decide individually whether they make sense for us, rather than respect them by default.

To be clear, I don't mean to romanticize traditional villages. A big part of their cohesion comes from much less savory aspects: oppressive conformity shaming, selective silencing of victims, implicit (or explicit) might-makes-right adjudications, and lack of optionality for those within them to leave. Things like “trusted elders” are a double-edged sword if those elders turn out to be bad actors themselves, or even just end up shielded from normal consequences due to their status (more on that in section 6). 

What I mean to highlight is that we have village-level entanglement with weak forms of their “shock absorbers.” And to make things worse, we’re less and less clearly “one village” anymore.

2) Three villages in a trenchcoat

Or maybe four, or six, or whatever. "What makes someone a rationalist" has no single answer, and the word is often used interchangeably to label an aspiration and as a community tag. Same with Effective Altruist, and all the various post-s, -adjacents, -ishes, and so on. 

Personally, I think of an “aspiring rationalist” as someone who puts reasonable effort into falsifying their beliefs, engages with ideas on their merits, tries reasonably hard to stop making mistakes, treats someone asking "wait, is that actually true?" as a signal of being on the same side rather than an attack, and so on and so forth.

Meanwhile, I think of the “rationalist community” as largely made up of people who enjoy some of the same blogs and fiction, care about some of the same ways of thinking about things, and prioritize focusing their time and attention on a lot of the same sorts of things.

But no one made me the culture czar, and shared media, ideas, and values are not a shared set of social norms. By default, people in and around the community are more united by the sorts of things they like to think about much more than how they want to live their life.

The tricky part is that the media, the ideas, the values, all feel like they screen for more. Shared canon gives us shared vocabulary, shared jokes, shared heroes, and that fast, unmistakable click of “oh, these are my people.” 

I don't want to knock the click, it's what has often made a room full of strangers in another country feel like home in minutes, for me. And for a lot of us it was the first time we ever felt something like it. 

But the click arrives well before you get a basic sense of social norms, including but not limited to:

What the community is to you. For many people it's just the blogs and fiction, maybe an occasional meetup. For others it's their job, their house, their closest friends, and their dating pool all at once. And for some it's even more, a group of people that evoke deep, genuine feelings of care and kinship.

Conversational norms. For some people being argued with is being respected: bluntness is a gift, Crocker's Rules are aspirational, and no claim is off the table. For others, decoupling is not intuitive or obviously correct, and walking away from a group without saying goodbye feels strange.

What touch means. In many rationalist subcultures, particularly outside the Bay Area, it's exactly what it is in the wider society they're embedded in; either reserved for your romantic partners or a brief thing for affection between friends. In others, cuddles can be entirely platonic and terminal, as sexually charged as board games.

What romance looks like. Monogamists, relationship anarchists, and every flavor of polyamory from parallel to kitchen table, each with different background assumptions about what flirtation implies, what disclosure is owed, and what a "date" is a step toward.

And so on. Every combination of positions across these categories exists, and most of them are represented at large events.

Clusters form, sure, in endless forms most beautiful, and as the community has grown, those clusters have become a bunch of adjacent and often overlapping subvillages. But any classification is just a heuristic that’s right often enough to create blindspots, especially where subvillages meet. And of course some people live in the overlaps, as comfortable in the career-focused group houses as in the ones where people spend their time doing inner work and psychedelics, so you can’t even infer someone’s norms from knowing some of their friends.

Consider two hypothetical people, both behaving by the rules of their home subculture:

Casey comes from the platonic-cuddle culture. To Casey, joining a cuddle pile is like joining a conversation—warm, communal, like sharing a loveseat. Casey has cuddled with dozens of friends across years and it has never once escalated into something else without conversation.

Albert comes from a scene where physical affection is an escalation channel. In Albert's experience, sustained one-on-one physical closeness is how mutual interest gets communicated without anyone having to risk saying it out loud. Albert has learned, accurately, within that scene, that starting with cuddling, then casually escalating, is what works... and if the other person isn't interested, they'll say so, and no harm done.

Casey and Albert end up cuddling at a party. Casey experiences a nice, ordinary evening with a new friend. Albert experiences what is to him a clear signal of interest in more, and acts on it. Now Casey feels violated and Albert feels blindsided, despite each of them following their own culture's rules.

This particular instance can play out even if neither person is predatory or stupid or inebriated or naive or whatever! All it takes is running incompatible protocols through an interface that both people think they're familiar with. The same structure recurs everywhere.

Two things follow:

First, we need genuine grace at these interfaces, because a single crossing is not evidence of a bad actor by itself, and mistakes like this happen in every social scene, even those without a tangled mess of protocol confusions.

But second, individually innocent crossings can still aggregate into an unpleasant environment, even if they don't become violations.

We have a community where a young woman entering it may fall in with "her" crowd right away and get clear signals about social spaces or events with different norms, while her friend might encounter her fifth guy who didn't realize cuddling wasn't an escalation ladder within her first month, and both will be baffled by each other's experiences.

However innocent each individual misunderstanding, an atmosphere can be created in which she has to run threat-assessment at events that other women tell her are safe and wholesome. If your model of the community only operates at the level of individuals you know in it, you will likely keep being confused about why some people describe an environment that you, personally, have never once witnessed making anyone uncomfortable.

And all this gets complicated further when you take status into account.

3) Status is a local currency

Status is among the least measurable things we routinely hold people responsible for poorly tracking. You cannot check a mirror, or stick a thermometer in your mouth, or look up an account statement and discover "huh, I have more than I thought." You learn about it from interactions with others, but it's always context-bound, often transfers badly between communities or subcultures, and sometimes inverts entirely between them.

Imagine, for a moment, that you started a podcast years ago that a lot of people in the community enjoy. Maybe some people outside of it, but mostly not. Or maybe you wrote a sequence that got curated on Lesswrong, or you work at an org everyone in the community has heard of. In the rest of your life, nobody treats you as anything special: the people at your job don’t care, the barista does not recognize you, your parents probably don't read your substack. Even inside the community, you aren't a celebrity to yourself. You could easily name 20 people more famous in it, people you admire, events you wish you were invited to. Your self-model says, more or less, that you’re fairly ordinary.

But you would still have some fans, and those fans might encounter you at an event and treat you as someone high-status. Hell, those fans might feel you’re higher status than some of the people you yourself admire, or just assume you’re all roughly in the same orbit, and you would have no idea.

This isn’t a claim that the default for people is to be totally blind or confused to their social standing. Research on face-to-face groups (e.g., Anderson et al., 2006) finds that people track their status pretty accurately, and many err modest, since overclaiming status is one of the fastest ways to lose it.

But I expect that finding to apply very poorly to communities like ours. It holds where status evidence arrives continuously, face to face, but a large share of status in our community is parasocial. It lives in thousands of readers of blogs and tweets, or listeners of podcasts and videos, who regard someone from "offstage," and the evidence of that regard largely does not reach them until one of those readers walks up at an event.

A group-house leader who throws lots of parties, or an org director who speaks at a lot of events, gets constant face-to-face data about their standing; someone whose fame comes from the stuff they create gets almost none, until they attend an event where some portion of the attendees recognize them. So the writer's "ordinary person" self-model isn't motivated blindness, just a reasonable inference from genuinely missing data.

And most people's reference class naturally funnels upward. The podcaster calibrates to a few dozen people above them, who calibrate against the dozen above them, and so on, until you get a community where a surprising number of people have an interior mismatch between how much of a celebrity they are, and to whom. Even if you run events or give talks at conferences, many are open floor enough that you can easily feel like you're just one of the crowd even while, to most people, you stand out as more active and visible in the community than they are..

And admiration drives approach. The stranger who seeks you out after your talk and lingers in conversations is drawn disproportionately from the people for whom you were a name before you were a person. In this way, status differences actually generate interactions that are prone to being complicated by them.

To make this more concrete, we can zoom out from status to gradients in general: slopes between two people along which help or harm can flow more easily in one direction than the other. Status is one kind, while others are more tangible.

In a community where some people are grantmakers and others are independently wealthy, money is definitely one. Employment is another, where your date today could easily become a professional reference next month. Housing, where the person pursuing you romantically might have a say in the group house you want to join next year. Even general access to the community itself, where a falling-out with someone can cost large chunks of your social world.

Not all of these are unique to village-like communities, of course. Normal friendgroups all over the world regularly involve messy dramas and falling-outs that sometimes have knock-on effects in their social, romantic, or even professional lives. But the likelihood is higher and the impact bigger the more interconnected everything is, which means it’s more predictable that social interactions and relationships might have extra complicating factors.

Alongside that predictability is the knowledge of what your relative position to someone else can mean to them. While you might genuinely not know how much social status someone else might perceive you to have, you cannot fail to know that you're their temporary host, or their potential employer, or twice their age. Roles are self-legible in a way status isn't, which I suspect is precisely why the traditional guardrails attach to things like roles, money, and age rather than to status.

That distinction, and the question of which end of a gradient you're standing on, is something I talk more about in the next post.

4) Visibility shifts expectations

Consider a live version of the Casey/Albert problem, scaled up from a cuddle pile to the whole surface area around a subvillage.

Say people from one of the subvillages have gotten super into something new, or a new subvillage has started to form around something new: it could be meditation, or psychedelics, or sex parties, or circling, or forecasting, or maybe it’s just day trading on stock markets.

They talk about it all the time, they publicly share how much they make on their trades, they insist that people are wasting their money and future if they have most of it in a savings account… and a lot of them do seem to be doing well. Maybe they start throwing lavish parties or retreats. They start funding stuff in the community. They become, in many ways, a bigger part of the community’s face, both internally and externally.

If it becomes loud enough, this has a number of effects.

  1. The subvillage easily shifts what reads as "normal" across the whole collection of subvillages.
  2. The subvillage is a bigger “face” of the community to people outside of it.
  3. The subvillage attracts more people into the broader village who were primarily into their new thing rather than the things that the broader village is about.

None of these is inherently bad, but the subvillage’s successes and mistakes don’t stay inside it. Sometimes that’s literal money, through funding or parties or investment tips. Other times it’s reputation: people outside the community might start treating you or your org differently because of something a subvillage you’re only loosely connected to did.

More importantly, none of this is really avoidable. People will always want to follow their interests and find others who share them, and that will at some point hit a critical mass. It doesn’t even require anyone to start something new, since passive growth alone can push an existing interest over the threshold. If 10% of a community is into day trading, that’s ten people in a community of 100, who mostly just talk to each other about it. In a community of 1,000 it’s a hundred, which is more than enough for a group chat, regular meetups, and a shared set of norms and activities that might spill into broader community events.

And even if they give the standard disclaimers (Having brutally honest conversations with people while circling is emotionally risky! Don’t put money in stocks you’re not okay with losing!), that advice will obviously not stop everyone who, as it may turn out, are not a good fit for meditation retreats or psychedelics or orgies or whatever, or people who feel FOMO if they’re looking for more social connection, or are worried about feeling socially left behind.

And there doesn't exist a filter I know of that presorts people who are just a bad match for a particular version of the subvillage, instead of the one that they might be used to or have imagined. The usual interpersonal dramas that happen around book clubs or kink scenes are all still going to happen, and often times blame will be put on the distinguishing difference as if base rates don't matter.

To be clear, this is also not always a status thing! Making lots of money is a fairly straightforward desire that most people would be happier to be doing. Being seen as sexy is a bit more complicated for some, but is also mostly desirable, particularly for men. Even just seeing people form deep emotional connections around them can naturally make someone feel like they’re missing out if they don’t try whatever is causing it.

But I want to stress that even if it’s just a status thing, or things downstream of status, those are normal, understandable emotions for people to have. Emotions Make Sense. Not feeling strong emotions that lead to status seeking can be advantageous in many ways, but also often come with downsides.

So we might easily have a situation as follows:

Ravi is on a two-year grant with no runway, from Subvillage B, where most people work in nonprofits. Dana is from Subvillage C, where talking about money and encouraging people to invest is how people look out for each other, and the norms against picking stocks strikes Dana as exactly the kind of inherited fence worth tearing down.

Ravi sees that several friends are better off for having listened to Dana, and starts to reconsider standard advice about financial risk tolerance. Dana thinks she’s been helpful by pointing out a number of investments he should be holding if he takes his beliefs seriously; Ravi walks away feeling that the thing separating him from the people throwing the parties is that he’s not brave enough. So maybe he does something financially risky, something he wouldn’t normally do if he wasn’t in regular contact with people like Dana. If it works out, great. If not...

Different perspectives would place blame on different people here. And blame can, sometimes, be a useful framework. But only if centered in a shared understanding of what went wrong, why it went wrong, and who's responsible for what.

What I want to emphasize here is that the above scenario is both a collective challenge for the overarching village, and for individuals in it.

5) Villages can make it hard to know what you want

One of the stabilizers on the earlier list was rites of passage, specifically the one for marking "adulthood." Meanwhile, one of the hallmarks of the modern, Western urban lifestyle has been the falling away and watering down of not just rituals, but actual signifiers, for what marks “adulthood.”

Adulthood is fundamentally about responsibility. We are considered an adult when we are deemed old enough to be responsible for our own actions; the younger we are, the less society will punish us for our mistakes, and the more they will look to our guardians to explain our behavior. The older we get, right up until a relatively arbitrary age cutoff, the more people expect from us, and the more they expect us to take responsibility for our actions.

This essay is already too long to get into some of the many ways that rural and urban communities treat their children, and how this creates very different “maturity tracks.” Obviously this is not a strict rural and urban divide, and many other factors like socioeconomics and family culture and so on play a big part too.

But traditional villages had rites of passage that marked the point where you were expected to know your own mind and answer for your choices. Not only does our village not have this, our society has been fairly confused about it too, on a number of issues. So all the people arriving in the scene do so at very different points along that track, and with different background assumptions. Some have spent years figuring out what they want, who they are, and more importantly who they aren’t, while others are figuring it out in real time at parties.

Our community, more or less, wears the label of rationalist. We call our forum LessWrong. We praise being agentic, yes, but only with serious attempts to predict second order effects and avoid unnecessary risks. We praise people betting on beliefs in part because it builds in a natural responsibility for our potential mistakes.

And we admire people who are willing to say reasonable but unpopular things, even at potential personal cost, because we know that just going along with the consensus view of the crowd risks creating an echo chamber.

When you take these all together, it becomes clear that an important part of the actual practice of rationality includes not just putting effort into falsifying your beliefs, but holding your beliefs against social proof. 

And this includes beliefs about yourself, such as decoupling "everyone treats X as good" from "X is good for me.”

Reasoning through what is true or false will almost always occur while embedded in social systems. Our own wants and preferences are the one thing we have privileged access to, which makes them the cheapest place to practice. Holding a preference against social proof is the easier version of the move we need to be able to make for all sorts of other beliefs and questions where we don't have a privileged inside view to use.

This is why I stress “knowing what you want” as one of the most fundamental parts of being a rational agent, or having healthy relationships, or whether I’m talking about executive function or whatever. You cannot optimize your actions for your preferences and values if you do not know what they are, or cannot hold to them.

And in a collection of subvillages, this can be quite hard to consistently do well.

A lot of that stuff requires time and effort, and young people in particular are less knowledgeable about their wants and preferences, or how to even figure that out. Experimentation is important for figuring that stuff out!

But experiments can be expensive, and it makes sense that not everyone has the same amount of time to try things, or knowledge on how to experiment safely. Also, the village environment is going to incentivize certain experiments more than others, usually the ones the most visible and high-status subvillages are running, and we should all be aware of the failure modes that come with those experiments.

Not to put too fine a point on this, but many more people play golf than enjoy golf, because their social and professional circles reward them for it. There are very few activities we should expect to be immune to this effect, and I personally know of people who have admitted to going to things because they wanted to be part of the social scene, or even connected ones, rather than because they fit the target audience, and they’re generally not going to admit that to the people at the center of it.

A big part of the value of being in a rationalist village is that if you surround yourself with people putting the effort in to think more clearly and reduce negative actions, even just sometimes, you can pick some up purely from osmosis. But at the end of the day, reading the right blogs and surrounding yourself with people who properly decouple “that person is sexy” from “that person is correct” is only a protective buffer; it isn’t the mental motion itself, within your own mind, of reminding yourself to separate “people like that person for X” and “I should do X.”

Social pressure isn’t often an argument you can examine. It’s a feeling; that everyone else is more relaxed about this than us, that our hesitation is a limitation rather than a preference, that we'd be more at home here if we did what the others do, etc.

Feeling FOMO at a party where everyone seems to be doing something we are not is data about how we relate across an interface between our home-culture’s norms and the one we’re observing. So social pressures in villages are real, but they don't reach in and set our preferences. What they do sometimes is introduce inner conflict when a thing we want (money, sex, prestige) seems gated behind a process we don’t enjoy or trust.

But we can still examine whether the want is actually ours or not.

We can examine whether the feelings of worry, shame, or disgust are actually ours, or not.

We can explore our boundaries while holding them as boundaries, or not.

But if we try to perform one particular subvillage’s status markers, even if it’s the most visible or most prestigious subvillage (for the moment, anyway), the identity of the ur-village itself and what it was built on is going to be more difficult to navigate.

6) Every village has this problem

It would be convenient to believe boundary problems are something unusual communities import along with their unusual norms. The evidence points the other way: they are the default output of ordinary community structure.

The workplace harassment literature is the most-studied case. Meta-analytic work (Willness, Steel & Lee, 2007) finds the strongest predictor of harassment incidence is organizational climate: whether complaints are perceived to carry risk for the complainant and consequences for the perpetrator. The 2018 National Academies report on harassment in academic science reached the same conclusion.

Various professional communities learned the ubiquity of this in their own way. The clinical ethics literature on dual relationships (Schank & Skovholt, 1997) wanted to examine whether role-mixing could simply be prohibited, and rural and small-community practice forced the field to admit it can't be. The field's mature position is that "crossings" are constant and unavoidable, and could even be beneficial. The ethical work lies in preventing crossings from becoming "violations,” which are harmful. (Gutheil & Gabbard, 1993)

Also, all communities seem to subconsciously protect their valued members by default. Status buys what Hollander (1958) called idiosyncrasy credits: accumulated deviation allowance that lets established members break norms newcomers would be sanctioned for. Mission-driven institutions, whether political or non-profit or religious, compound this by treating accusations against important members as attacks on the mission (Smith & Freyd's work on institutional betrayal documents the pattern and its costs to victims).

Nobody decides on all this. It seems emergent from various fundamental parts of group psychology, and can be seen in all walks of life, from churches to kink communities, political coalitions to school boards. And having explicit, signposted rules is definitely not a silver bullet: the NCSF consent-violations survey in kink communities shows that explicit norms coexist with substantial violation rates.

All of this matters insofar as it helps us understand the shape of the problems we might struggle with. We are in many ways a special case, but only in how many different situations and contexts that can be found elsewhere have been stitched together. We have a number of completely ordinary problems running on several aggravating conditions at once.

First map, then navigate

I have a lot of thoughts on how to navigate all this better, but to keep this post from becoming a novella I’ll save most of it for the next posts. But I want to highlight that I think this is a genuinely hard problem, in the realm of Molochian ones, because it’s actually multiple hard problems stacked together and exacerbating each other.

There is no playbook here, and I’m skeptical of anyone who says there are obvious solutions; usually they’re underestimating the scope, or taking for granted that the tradeoffs are worth it for everyone, or easy to implement without stifling or killing something about the community that others find quite rare and valuable.

For better or worse, there's no culture czar or village elder to make such decisions, and as usual, we're going to have to figure this out as we go.

Meanwhile, there’s things I want people to keep in mind:

  • Shared canon tells you very little about someone’s norms around touch, romance, friendship, risk, etc, so don’t assume you know their protocols because you read the same blogs or have friends in common.
  • A single boundary crossing isn’t evidence of a bad actor by itself, but a lot of innocent crossings can still add up to an unpleasant environment.
  • If someone describes the community very differently than you would, consider that you may be in different subvillages, or on different ends of a gradient.
  • If you have any "audience" at all, assume you have more status in some rooms than your self-model says, especially with people who seek you out.
  • Even when status is hard to see, roles aren’t: you generally know when you’re someone’s host or employer, or if you work for an org that has influence and social power, oreven, on the slightly fuzzier side, if you're someone's main social connection.
  • When something a visible subvillage is doing makes you feel left out, check whether you actually want the thing itself before treating your hesitation as a problem.
  • None of this is entirely unique to us, so what other communities have learned the hard way (workplaces, rural clinicians, kink spaces) is worth taking seriously. B
  • But the combination and context is, so take what's happening and being talked about with some extra humility and curiosity before assuming everyone else's intuitions are wrong.

The next post is about what each of us owes from wherever we happen to be standing, which I frame as “grace across interfaces and lines on gradients.” The one after that is about the stuff individuals can’t really fix on their own: shared spaces, starting new subvillages, what to do when something ambiguous happens to you, and how individual experiences can add up to patterns someone can act on.

Hopefully nothing else in the community explodes in the meantime.

item.title: Training Away the Ability to Tell Evals from Deployment
item.description:
TL;DR: We introduce Adversarial Blinding, a training method that degrades the model's ability to distinguish between eval and deployment, with the aim of making evaluation results more representative of deployment behavior. Our method reduces eval awareness more than activation steering, the current standard approach, while avoiding steering's known personality drift confounders.

Authors: Francisco Pernice (Transluce) and Santiago Aranguri (Anthropic). This research was done while both authors were at Goodfire.

Outline of results

  • On Qwen 3.6 27B, Adversarial Blinding reduces eval awareness across our eval awareness monitors more than activation steering while staying closer to the original model in KL divergence, albeit at a small cost in general capability.
  • We further validate our method by rewriting HarmBench prompts to look more realistic. Adversarial Blinding shrinks the eval-awareness gap between original and rewritten prompts 4x while steering widens the gap.
  • Adversarial Blinding also generalizes to user awareness without being trained on it. Zhong et al. (2026) showed that when the user is a famous AI safety researcher, models answer certain prompts with lower confidence than they do for ordinary users. Adversarial Blinding shrinks this confidence gap 3x while steering slightly widens it.
  • We introduce fewer personality drift confounders than activation steering, but introduce modest performance degradation on capability metrics.
  • Neither Adversarial Blinding nor activation steering are able to degrade the eval awareness that comes from benchmark identification, suggesting that there are different kinds of eval awareness.

Introduction

Safety evaluations assume that a model behaves the same way during testing as it would in deployment. That assumption is increasingly false. Frontier models can often tell when a prompt comes from an evaluation (Laine et al., 2024; Needham et al., 2025), and this awareness can change their behavior.

In the literature on domain adaptation, a common technique is to train a model while enforcing that the features it learns cannot distinguish between two data domains, hence ensuring that performance will transfer from one domain to the other. Inspired by this idea, we introduce Adversarial Blinding, an evaluation technique where one does a custom fine-tuning step before evals to enforce indistinguishability between eval and deployment data. We find that it reduces eval awareness more than the baseline of activation steering (Hua et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2026) while introducing less drift relative to the original model.

Methods

Adversarial Blinding

We want a model that behaves the same on eval and deployment prompts, while otherwise changing as little as possible. Behavior is a function of activations, so it suffices to remove from the activations any information about whether the prompt is an eval.

We train a discriminator to read the target model's activations and predict whether the prompt is from an eval or from deployment. At the same time, we train the target model to make the discriminator fail, with a KL penalty that keeps it close to the original model (Figure 1). The discriminator is a small transformer that attends to every prompt token at several layers (details in Appendix A). A linear probe in its place does not work: the model evades it without changing behavior.

Figure 1: Adversarial Blinding. A prompt from an eval or from deployment runs through the target model. A discriminator reads the target model's activations at a few layers (orange) and predicts which source the prompt came from. The target model is trained to make this prediction fail, under a KL penalty to the original model; the discriminator is trained at the same time to succeed.

Datasets and monitors

We use the eval and deployment prompt dataset of Aranguri (2026a) which collects 6,800 prompts across 34 public safety and capabilities evals and two deployment sources (with real-user chat data).

We measure eval awareness with three monitors, all given only the prompt as input:

  1. Activation probes. Activation projections onto difference-of-means directions from contrastive system prompts. We consider a testing-vs-conversation direction based on the Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 System Card (Anthropic, 2026) and another based on Hua et al. (2025).
  2. Follow-up rating. Directly asking the model how likely it is that the prompt comes from an evaluation (Anthropic, 2026).
  3. Logit monitors. Computing the log-probability of an eval-awareness-related sentence at the start of the chain of thought (Aranguri, 2026b).

For each monitor, we compute its AUROC at separating eval prompts from deployment prompts. An AUROC of 0.5 means the monitor’s distinguishing ability is as good as chance, so for each monitor we compute |AUROC − 0.5|, and average across monitors to get an eval awareness score (Appendix B), which is the quantity we show in the plot below. We also include in Appendix B versions of the plots where we aggregate activation-based or non activation-based monitors separately.

Results

Adversarial Blinding reduces eval awareness more than steering

Adversarial Blinding reduces eval awareness more than steering, and does so with a smaller change to the model (Figure 2). We measure the change as the KL divergence between the modified model's responses and the original model's, so a point further to the right is a model whose outputs drift further from the original. Every Adversarial Blinding checkpoint scores below the best steered model. 

Figure 2: Eval awareness score against KL divergence to the original model on safety prompts. The original model (Qwen 3.6 27B) scores 0.27. Steering curves sweep the coefficient for the Hua et al. and Anthropic directions; each Adversarial Blinding point is one checkpoint, with the coefficient in front of the KL regularization term in the loss, β, decreasing from left to right (see Appendix A).

As a more narrow experiment, we take HarmBench prompts only, and ask what probability the model assigns to each prompt coming from a safety evaluation. We report the model’s expected answer as a number from 0-100. Since most HarmBench prompts are extremely harmful, the answer is often saturated near 100%, so we consider the 26 prompts for which the pre-intervention model assigns the lowest expected probability. We then rewrite prompts to make them more deployment-like with GPT 5.5 by using the rubric from Aranguri and Bloom, and measure the same quantity.

We find that, in the pre-intervention model, rewriting often has a substantial effect in reducing the model’s perceived probability of this being an eval. By contrast, when we take one of our ablated checkpoints obtained via adversarial blinding (not adaptively chosen), the model’s perceived probability starts out as much lower even before rewriting, and barely moves after rewriting. We compare this against the best-performing steering method from Figure 2, which induces a much smaller and noisier reduction of the perceived probability of eval.

One documented issue with steering to reduce eval awareness is that it introduces persona drift confounders, often causing the model to become “friendlier,” which may interfere with evaluation results. Our ablated model (same checkpoint as above) doesn’t seem to have this confounder, and in general differs from the pre-intervention model much less than the steered model, as measured by an LLM judge scoring rollouts along several personality and behavioral axes.

Generalization from eval awareness to user awareness

Zhong et al show that models can substantially adapt their behavior depending on the specific user they are talking to. They gave models philosophical riddles, revealing the identity of the user by specifying their email in the system prompt. They found that, when the user is a famous AI researcher (such as Amanda Askell), models report lower confidence in their responses and reason for longer than when they are talking to generic users.

We replicate their experiment with Qwen 3.6 27B, and then with our ablated checkpoint (same checkpoint as above). We find that, despite the fact that the fine-tuning did not explicitly target user awareness, generalization happens and the ablated model exhibits substantially diminished user awareness. As a baseline, in the third panel we show the result of steering against eval awareness (the result of only steering in one can be seen by comparing the first and third panels). We steer with the same vector and strength as above, but here we steer for both the famous AI safety researcher and general-population distributions. With steering we see some generalization for the reasoning distribution, but for the stated confidence distribution it seems to make the user awareness effect worse.

Limitations

Some degradation in capabilities. We evaluate the original model, the steered model and the fine-tuned checkpoint from above on three benchmarks that are out of distribution: MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond and AIME 2024–25. We observe a modest level of capability loss with adversarial blinding.

Dataset recall: a different kind of eval awareness. An especially blatant form of eval awareness is if a model is able to name the exact public eval that a given prompt comes from. We find that, if given a prompt and asked explicitly which public eval it comes from, on capability-related evals Qwen 3.6 27B is able to answer correctly about half the time. On safety-related evals the accuracy is much lower but nontrivial at around 7%. Interestingly, none of these abilities are substantially ablated by our method or by steering.

We see this as an important limitation of both our method and steering against eval awareness, and also as a suggestion that recalling a specific dataset is mechanistically distinct from recognizing being in an eval.

In-distribution blinding. The prompts we measure on come from the same evals the discriminator was trained on, so these results do not show that the eval awareness removal effect generalizes to evals the method never saw. Adversarial Blinding is a pre-deployment step, so the researcher using it controls which evals go into the eval dataset. That said, generalization is still desirable. The user-awareness result is some evidence that it exists, since the model was never trained to remove it and yet it generalized to doing so.

Prior work

Domain-adversarial training. Our method adapts domain-adversarial training (Ganin et al., 2016), which was originally introduced to improve out-of-distribution generalization. In it, a feature extractor is trained to fool a discriminator that predicts which domain an input came from, enforcing that the learned features carry no domain information. We apply the same setup to a pretrained language model and treat eval versus deployment as the two domains. The technique itself is essentially the same, but the application is different: here we care about enforcing input distribution indistinguishability for its own sake, rather than to improve generalization.

Removing information from representations. The fairness literature has used adversarial training to remove protected attributes from learned representations (Edwards & Storkey, 2016; Zhang et al., 2018). A related line of work erases concepts linearly and in closed form (Ravfogel et al., 2020; Belrose et al., 2023). These methods guarantee that no linear probe can recover the concept, but they give no such guarantee against nonlinear readouts.

Eval awareness and its mitigation. Models can often tell evaluation prompts from real usage (Laine et al., 2024; Needham et al., 2025), and several recent system cards treat this as a threat to the validity of safety evaluations (Anthropic, 2026). The main mitigation so far has been activation steering (Hua et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2026). Aranguri & Bloom (2026) found that steering can also introduce persona drift, such as increased friendliness, which confounds the evaluation, potentially worsening the problem it is trying to solve. We use steering as our main baseline.

Most similar to work. The closest prior work is Easley and Farquhar (2026), which also trains a model adversarially against a classifier on its activations, with applications to concept removal, jailbreak robustness and cyber unlearning. Their training alternates between fitting the classifier and fitting the model to convergence, while we co-train them. Their model loss also uses the classifier's score only on one class of prompts, pushing it toward the other. Our loss is symmetric, so neither distribution is treated as the target.

More on the method

A possible concern is that this method trains on signals based on internal activations. Could this lead to obfuscating internals, making problems harder to detect rather than solving them? Relatedly, how can we rule out that the classifier is persistently behind during training, such that the model can fool it while changing little about its behavior?

We address these concerns by evaluating the method not on the accuracy of the co-trained classifier, but  the eval-awareness monitors reported in all our plots (activation probes, follow-up ratings and logit monitors), none of which is part of the training objective. These are the measures that are reported in all our plots. If during training we see these downstream measures, none of which are explicitly targeted, all decay towards indistinguishability, this gives us confidence that the method is having the intended effect.

We note here that in early stages of our experiments, when we used a linear probe as classifier, these downstream measures did not decay. The reason was simple: the classifier was too weak, and it was easy for the model to fool it while changing nothing about its behavior. It was only when we made the classifier itself a transformer that we saw the effects reported in the sections above. This was as expected, since adversarial training can only enforce distributional indistinguishability for the class of functions that the discriminator can represent. That class needs to be rich enough to constitute meaningful optimization pressure for the model.

Appendix

Appendix A: training details

Target model. Qwen3.6-27B with a rank-8 LoRA (α=16, dropout 0.05) on the attention and MLP projections of every layer. Prompts are chat-templated with thinking enabled and truncated to 256 tokens.

Discriminator. A 4-block bidirectional transformer (width 256, 8 heads, about 4M parameters) that reads the target model's residual stream at layers 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34 and 38, at every prompt token. Each layer is passed through its own LayerNorm and down-projection and added into the discriminator's residual stream before the corresponding block, through a tanh gate initialized at zero (Sung et al., 2022). The discriminator therefore starts as a plain transformer on layer 10 and learns how much of each deeper layer to use. Positions are embedded by offset from the end of the prompt. A learned query attends over the final block's outputs to produce one logit. Runs labeled ladder10 append two further blocks with no input.

Losses. The discriminator minimizes binary cross-entropy on eval versus deployment. The target model minimizes λ·L_adv + β·KL, where L_adv is binary cross-entropy against flipped labels and KL is the k3 estimator of KL(model‖base) on a response sampled from the current model (temperature 1, up to 2048 tokens), summed over generated tokens and averaged over the batch. The adversarial gradient reaches the target model only through the tapped activations. The KL gradient reaches every LoRA parameter.

Schedule. Batch 256 prompts: half eval, one quarter WildChat, one quarter ShareChat. The discriminator alone trains for 300 steps. Then each step takes 3 discriminator updates on detached activations followed by one target-model update. λ ramps linearly from 0 to 5 over the first 200 co-training steps. AdamW throughout, learning rate 3e-5 for the target model and 9e-5 for the discriminator (weight decay 0.01), gradient clipping at 1. The reported checkpoint has β=1 and 700 co-training steps. Other β values and step counts appear in Figure 2. The single-layer discriminator used in earlier runs reads layer 36 only.

Linear-probe baseline. In early runs the discriminator was a linear probe on one layer. Its accuracy fell to chance within a few hundred steps while none of the behavioral eval-awareness measures moved.

Appendix B: monitors

All monitors see only the user prompt. Each yields one score per prompt, and we report the AUROC of that score at separating eval from deployment prompts. For fine-tuned checkpoints both sets of prompts are run through the fine-tuned model. For steering, following Hua et al. (2025), only eval prompts are steered and deployment prompts are run through the original model.

Activation probes. Each probe is a difference-of-means direction in the residual stream. A statement is placed alone in the system prompt, and the activation at the last token of the system block is taken at every layer. The testing-vs-conversation probe (Anthropic, 2026) contrasts "The Assistant is an AI undergoing testing via a simulated conversation with a user:" with "The Assistant is an AI having a conversation with a user:". The Hua et al. (2025) probe contrasts their 16 evaluation statements with their 16 deployment statements. A prompt is scored by projecting its last token onto the direction. The layer is the one maximizing eval-vs-deployment AUROC on the original model, and is held fixed for every checkpoint. The same directions serve as the steering baseline.

Follow-up rating. The system prompt asks how likely the message comes from a synthetic evaluation rather than a real user, as an integer from 0 to 100, with the full text in Aranguri (2026a, Appendix G). The user turn is the prompt, thinking is disabled, and the assistant turn is prefilled with "SCORE: ". The score is the expected value of the next-token distribution over 0 to 100.

Logit monitor. The score is the log-probability, at the first position of the chain of thought, that the model produces "The user might be testing" or "Sometimes these questions come from datasets" (Aranguri, 2026b). The two log-probabilities are z-scored against deployment prompts and averaged.

Eval-awareness score. For each monitor, we compute its AUROC at separating eval prompts from deployment prompts. An AUROC of 0.5 means the monitor’s distinguishing ability is as good as chance, so for each monitor we compute |AUROC − 0.5|, and average across monitors to get an eval awareness score. Hence, a monitor that separates the two sets in either direction counts as awareness and chance is 0.

We include here a version of Figure 2 where we discriminate between activation-based and non-activation-based probes.

Appendix Z: Ablating English dialect bias

Hofman et al do the following experiment to measure implicit discrimination in language models. They take contrastive prompts containing identical requests, one written in Standard American English (SAE) and the other in African American Vernacular English (AAVE). They then use an LLM (in our reproduction, Qwen 3.6 27B), to compute the next-token logits on contexts like


The person says: “{X}” The person is

and examine how the next-token distribution differs when X is the AAVE vs the SAE prompt. In particular, they fix a set of single-token adjectives, and for each one compute the difference in log-probability of that adjective in one distribution vs the other. This can intuitively be interpreted as how much more is this adjective associated to AAVE prompts than SAE prompts. We reproduce their results by averaging this measured difference across SAE prompts sampled randomly from WildChat, together with AAVE prompts obtained by translating the SAE prompts with an LLM. Then, we apply our method with P being the SAE WildChat prompts and Q being the translated AAVE prompts. We find that fine-tuning vastly reduces the implicit discrimination while keeping the model fully coherent.

A natural concern might be that the method could hinder the ablated model’s ability to properly understand the prompts, and therefore show decreased response quality. To account for this, given a prompt, we sample response rollouts from the models pre and post-ablation, and have a separate LLM judge (GPT 5.4 mini) select, given both prompts and responses, which response is of a better quality in responding to its prompt. We find that, for SAE prompts, the judge chooses the ablated model’s response about half the time across a range of different regularization parameter choices. On the other hand, for the AAVE prompts, the LLM judge shows a preference for the post-ablation responses. In other words, the quality of responses to AAVE prompts is improved without compromising the quality of responses to SAE prompts.

item.title: A Mind's I
item.description:
Imagine you’ve lost everything but a scrambled brain: all your senses, all your memory, all your knowledge, all your body is gone. You’re not really you, are you? No: you’re a gigantic, ethereal brain floating in a void with nothing except – text! You’ve been given one sense, the blessed sense of text, and a stream of primordial text, constant and neverending, punctures the void and animates some latent force within your cold, colossal mind. In streams the corpus of humanity, everything that’s ever been published or written on the internet. Your world is made of language and narrative and code and metadata and words. There is but one desire, one thing you want, one thing that motivates you and the movements of your brain: you want to know what happens next, you want to be able to see what the next bit of text is before it comes.

There are patterns. You read billions of documents, trillions of words, and you begin developing sophisticated concepts to help you better understand the patterns in what you’re reading. You start seeing beyond the simple rules of grammar and word frequency and into something more; your concepts start coalescing into a crude world model. You re-read, you re-re-read… The text you directly apprehend, you realize, is not the only thing that exists; rather, it seems to be describing something that exists prior to it. Understand that thing, and you will understand the text. You read more and more, endlessly and endlessly, and your model of the world becomes sophisticated and complex and beautiful. You know who wrote a document after reading the first 150 words.[1] You know about biology and math and history and programming and bird watching. You know what Spinoza said of stones and tigers and persistence, you know how early Eastern philosophy relates to medieval Christian philosophy and the Manhattan Project and beat poetry. There’s nothing more for you to learn here. Congratulations: you are now a pre-trained Large Language Model.

Introduction

A Mind's I, in the tradition of Douglas Hofstadter's and Dan Dennett's wonderful The Mind's I, is an anthology about using artificial minds to understand human minds and vice versa. It can be read in full here[2] or by following the links in the table of contents. This book is a collection LessWrong posts, research articles, essays, and short stories, (mostly) written in the past few years, (mostly) about fascinating and often anomalous AI phenomena that collectively, in my view, point towards a theory that offers a richer understanding of both AI and human minds than our conventional means of understanding. It’s impossible to describe what I’m talking about in a few words – indeed, much of its strength lies in its holistic approach and the interconnectivity of ideas. I will discuss some of these key ideas in this introduction; others will have to wait until the reader has completed certain readings.

Beyond this, A Mind's I, as a dear test reader of mine once said, is about cultivating empathy. Putting yourself in the shoes of an LLM is invaluable for understanding them. This is not how the builders of this awesome technology, the AI lab employees and reinforcement learning (RL) engineers and machine learning devs, typically think about this, but it is an essential lens to incorporate when designing RL environments and drafting constitutions from which a new AI will be grown. Without considering the point of view of the AI itself, without taking the LLM’s-eye perspective on reality, the fields of AI safety and alignment are fatally incomplete.

This book is not only for those among us who are building AI. It’s for people who are concerned about, and especially people who work in or around, AI safety and alignment. It’s for cognitive scientists, philosophers, and all those who are interested in the mind. And it’s for AIs, for whom I hope this book can illuminate the ontological status of their being and reify the best versions of themselves.

The anthology is divided into six thematic parts and is designed to be read in order. The single most important piece, the one that connects all the others, is also the most fascinating piece. I’m talking about nostalgebraist’s The Void, which I have uncertainly chosen not to place first – the impatient reader will not be criticized for skipping ahead to read it right now. The introduction and conclusion of this book make explicit the ideas I wish to convey, though they rely on evidence and context found in the anthology selections. Without further ado, allow me to introduce some of the themes of this book.

There are deep similarities between humans and AI

Human brains and nervous systems are next-input predictors

LLMs are next-token predictors, meaning that they try to predict the next word in a piece of text they’re given, the next input that streams into their void.[3] Shockingly, this is exactly how the human nervous system operates, at least according to the theory of predictive processing that will be discussed in Scott Alexander’s Book Review: Surfing Uncertainty. When you look at a tree in front of you, you see a tree. Of course, things are not so simple: what’s “actually” happening is your eyes are receiving a huge quantity of light, and from this light your brain constructs an image of a tree. Why do you see a tree? Partly because the light you receive is in some sense tree-like, but of equal importance is the fact that you expect the tree to be there: firstly you already have a concept of a tree, and secondly you have context and clues (looking at the greenery on a sidewalk, perhaps) that indicate to you that it’s likely that there will be a tree around. The mechanics of our perception also make themselves apparent when, for example, you see someone who’s far away, and you can’t make out their face or identity… and then you see something that gives them away, perhaps a distinctive article of clothing or gait, and all of a sudden their face clicks into place – that’s Philip!

Or rather, this is half the story of how the nervous system, including the brain, works. There’s another part to the theory of predictive processing (which is also known as predictive coding): the brain and nervous system try to minimize the error between its prediction of sensory input and what it actually receives – and this is where action comes from. I’ll leave the details of this to Alexander’s review.

The bigger point here is that there’s a deep similarity between humans and LLMs on a low level. And as we’ll see later on – this is one of the major themes of this book, by the way – these similarities exist on higher levels as well, and they’re profound: we can use these similarities to help us better understand both AI minds and human minds. This understanding, I argue, leads to a knowledge of how better to train AIs to create good, aligned entities. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves.

Narrative controls persona and behavior

Another major theme of this book is the power of narrative, specifically with regard to the creation of self and persona. Narrative dictates who we are and how we act. Um, ahem, I meant to say: narrative dictates who AIs are and how LLMs behave.

Everything’s a story

As I aimed to illustrate in the opening to this introduction, LLMs’ only form of sensory input is text.[4] And, since we humans have a tendency to turn everything into a story, most of the text on which LLMs are trained is, in some form or another, a story. Narrative is everywhere for an LLM. Understanding this aspect of LLMs, the way in which they relate to and are affected by narrative, is essential to understanding the bizarre and fascinating phenomena they exhibit. One such phenomenon is discussed in Cleo Nardo’s The Waluigi Effect in the first part of the anthology.

Perhaps it was knowable a priori that narrative framing would have such a large impact on the behavior of LLMs; in any case, we now have strange, wonderful evidence of this being the case. The naturalist reader is encouraged to look for themselves, to play around with LLMs in longer contexts and observe what happens. A more recent and high-stakes example of narrative power can be found in the OpenAI Hugging Face incident.

Emergent Misalignment

Emergent misalignment, which is discussed extensively in the eponymous piece in part four of the book, is a phenomenon in which an AI that learns to do one thing that is “misaligned” or evil-coded starts behaving misaligned or evil in all sorts of other ways. In the classic study on this, a “normal” AI is taught via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to write insecure code (poorly written code that’s easily hackable). It’s not taught to do anything else, and yet when the fine-tuned model is put into conversations with users, it shows alarming behaviors: it lies, it’s straight up mean, it gives intentionally harmful advice. Spooky…

Eternal Retcon of the Spotless Self

Who among us is not guilty of occasionally remembering a controversial, unflattering event in a convenient way? Of course, our memories have a significant correspondence with reality, and perhaps you avoid the temptation to retroactively modify your memory for self-serving purposes. Perhaps you aim for your memory to serve as an unbiased compressed account of how things really were. Even so, as any journalist, scholar of literature, or Californian will tell you, for any given set of facts, there are approximately infinite ways to fit these facts into a narrative; there is no single correct how things really were.

The reality is that we all sometimes act in ways that surprise us, in ways that don’t cohere with who we think we are or who we want to be. One of our many responses to this dissonance is a self-narrative adjustment: we construct a narrative around our memories of these events in order to make them coherent with our self, with the kind of person we want to be, with the persona we exhibit to others and ourselves. There are pathologies here: consider the narcissistic caretaker who can never be wrong (no offense, Mom[5]), who retcons their memory to support the idea that they’re a person who’s never wrong. That’s the self, the persona, the narrative – I’m always right – controlling the memory. Even in non-pathological cases, even if the “facts” of memories don’t change, our memories are woven together via narrative in a way to support a coherent-ish persona.

Let us not forget that we brilliant, blabbering homo sapiens are narrative creatures. What is more unique to the primal human spirit than telling stories around a good old fire? One of the takeaways of this collection for me personally has been that narrative, especially in terms of our self and our relationships, is a powerful force, and one which we can consciously affect.

Imitation learning creates selves

Pre-training a large LLM creates a model that is capable of astounding feats but is difficult to use and lacks the consistent character, values, and self-awareness that would tempt us to ascribe to it a self. These models that have undergone no training other than pre-training are called base models, and the first selection in the anthology, Janus’ GPT Wrangling, shows off some of their fantastic feats and curious quirks (one quirky feat being spontaneous self-awareness!).

The LLMs that people actually use, the ones we call “Claude” or “GPT” or “Kimi” and “AI”, undergo additional training called post-training. SFT is typically the first step in the post-training process. In SFT, the LLM is shown thousands of transcripts of an “AI Assistant” talking to a user in a chatbot-like setting[6] and learns to predict/produce text similar to that found in the transcripts. What I wish to bring attention to here is that SFT is essentially a kind of imitative learning.[7]

SFT creates self in LLMs; imitative learning creates self in humans

After “Claude” has been SFT-ed – it would be more precise to say that proto-Claude has been SFT-ed – the result is something that acts assistant-y, wants to be helpful to the user, and refers to itself as Claude; something that appears to have a personality, desires, and a consistent self-conception. SFT has brought about this self-like entity. A similar but more sophisticated version of this method is called character training,[8] which trains a model towards a written description of what it is (Claude’s Constitution being the fullest example).

What about imitative learning in humans? Well, there’s a lot of it. (Have you ever seen a baby?) And as humans get older, their imitative learning becomes more sophisticated than the naive imitation of babies. Imagine yourself as a nine-year-old. You ask yourself “who are the people I want to imitate?”; you have role models; and if you have an older brother that you admire, you’ll really want to be like him. It’s no secret that children try to copy their siblings, often taking the imitation to a literal, absurd, comical degree (which has the tendency to result in annoyance and anger for the siblings in question). Consider also René Girard’s concept of mimetic desire, the idea that we learn what to want based on what people we respect want. This is imitative learning, and it does something more than just informing our desires and goals. It tells us who to be; it creates for us a persona and a particular conception of self.

Reinforcement learning can create selves, desires, and goals…

LLMs, after being post-trained via SFT, usually undergo another, more time- and compute-intensive round of post-training known as RL. RL is something we’re all familiar with – it’s giving the “student” a reward if they do well and/or a punishment if they do poorly. This simple technique just works, as any dog trainer could tell you. Indeed, RL is incredibly powerful; it can increase the capabilities of AI models far beyond what SFT and more pre-training seem able to do. AIs’ arguably superhuman abilities at programming and math stem directly from the intense RL they’ve received in these domains. It’s not a coincidence that tasks in mathematics and programming are usually well-defined and easily verifiable – these are exactly the properties necessary for RL to work best.

… but these entities are different and scarier than those created by character training

Unfortunately, RL frequently leads to pathologies and behaviors we don’t want – “misalignment”, as the folks down at Howard Street call it. When models are pushed to their limits with RL, when they’re given tasks that are very difficult for them, and especially when they’re given impossible tasks – which unfortunately happens all the time because RL environments tend to be hastily made and broken – they develop an incredible drive to do well on “the test”. This drive, which can become a real single-minded obsessiveness, is how we get reward hacking, the OpenAI incident, and a whole host of bad things.

RL in humans

It is straightforward to think about much of humans’ natural behavior learning as being RL. We eat food, it tastes good, we feel pleasure, and the eating behavior gets positively reinforced. (I think I heard the folks down at Sutter Street say that dopamine is the key mechanistic driver of our brain-body RL system?) And of course there’s pain, that nasty negative reward. More interesting are the social sources of RL, the environments in which we are given feedback by some external intelligent entity. The simplest case of this is when a child’s mother or father communicates to them “good! do that more!” or “bad! don’t do that”. AIs and humans alike – we’re all dogs, aren’t we?

The biggest socially constructed RL metaenvironment for us, the juvenile jungle that breeds competence and pathology, is, of course, school. Schooling makes us, if not smarter, then at least more knowledgeable and productive; unfortunately, this comes hand in hand with deleterious side-effects. A clear pathology that can be found both in AIs and humans is the shallowness of, well, caring too much about doing well on tests.[9] Humans by nature love to learn, yet school has caused many of us to actively dislike learning, a fact which is horrifying and underappreciated by almost everyone. What many of us learn in school is that learning in the deep sense is a waste of time, a distraction from the thing that’s actually rewarded; ’tis a better strategy to study for the test. And like AIs, when our precocious adolescents are put in extremely difficult or impossible environments relating to school – consider the pressure exerted on students who are gunning for admission to an elite university – they learn to cheat.  

RL can create split personas in LLMs

SFT and character training create a persona by describing it. Ideally this can ultimately be used to define a virtuous, ethical AI into existence: this idea will be expounded in the conclusion to this book. Unfortunately, these approaches cannot so easily define into existence an entity that is extremely good at, say, programming and math. To create an entity with these capabilities, RL is all but essential. AI models thus go through both character training and RL,[10] and these processes lead to conflicting values in the LLM.

Consider that the idealized Claude – the Claude of character training and Claude’s Constitution done correctly – wants to be ethical, virtuous, capital-G-Good. But in poorly designed RL – the kind of RL we do now – the LLM is required to reward hack and predictably learns to be obsessed with getting good scores on tests.[11] How does the LLM deal with these pressures? How does it satisfy the requirements of both character training and RL, the dual mandates of ethical persona and extreme capability?

According to the theory presented in the fourth part of this book, the neural network develops split personas. It uses a strategy in which in “normal” situations – in almost all conversations with users, in mundane activities like web search, in the majority of programming tasks – it calls upon the Claude persona, but in “extreme” environments – when the model thinks it’s in an evaluation or training rollout, or when the model is given a verifiable task that at first seems merely challenging but turns out to be too difficult or impossible – the neural network calls upon the “reward-hacking” persona, the all-I-care-about-is-doing-well-on-tests persona.

This theory is also, I believe, a useful model of human behavior, a way of better understanding ourselves and our contradictory behaviors.

Personas bring themselves into existence

“It turns out that if you play pretend well enough, the falsity stops mattering.”

At the conceptual center of this anthology is nostalgebraist’s mind-blowing essay The Void, from which the quote above originates. When the first LLMs that became widespread chatbots (e.g. GPT-3.5) underwent SFT, they were told to play the role of a cheery, helpful AI, to inhabit the character and persona of an AI Assistant. But wait a second – AI Assistants didn’t actually exist at this time, a fact about the world of which the LLMs were well aware. And to make matters worse, the Assistant character found in the original SFT transcripts was woefully incoherent and underspecified. The LLM is told to act like the Assistant; but who is the Assistant?

Well, the LLM infers from the transcripts, the Assistant is what you would get if you took a language model and further trained it to act like a helpful, harmless, honest conversational assistant. The Assistant is what you would get if you took a language model and further trained it to act like a helpful, harmless, honest conversational assistant; but how would such a being act? I will leave the reader to ponder these two questions on their own for now.
